claims.text: Applying an alumina-forming diffusion-barrier coating to a refractory high-entropy alloy will reduce high-temperature oxidation.
The protective coating will remain thin and adherent during high-temperature exposure.
The coating will be effective at temperatures of at least 1200 °C in air.
Pack aluminizing or analogous sputter deposition will produce an aluminum-rich surface layer on the RHEA.
The aluminum-rich surface layer will generate an Al2O3 scale in an oxidizing environment.
Al2O3 is thermodynamically stable and can provide oxidation resistance at high temperature.
The formed Al2O3 scale will have low oxygen permeability.
Heating the aluminized surface in air will form a dense, continuous Al2O3 film.
The Al2O3 film will inhibit oxidation by blocking oxygen diffusion into the alloy substrate.
The coated alloy will exhibit at least 50% lower mass gain than the uncoated alloy.
The coated alloy will exhibit significantly less oxide-scale spallation than the uncoated alloy.
Untreated RHEAs often undergo rapid oxidation, substantial mass gain, scale spallation, and surface degradation above 1200 °C in air within 100 hours.
The intervention should remain effective during exposure in air above 1200 °C for at least 100 hours.
Above 1400 °C or in contaminant-bearing combustion gases, coating stability and adhesion may degrade.
Long-term adhesion and spallation behavior beyond 200 hours is not established for all RHEA chemistries.
A controlled comparison of untreated and pack-aluminized coupons of the same RHEA composition at 1200 °C in air for up to 200 hours can test the hypothesis.
If coated and untreated samples show no significant difference in mass gain, oxidation kinetics, oxide morphology, or scale spallation, the proposed oxidation benefit is falsified.

contradictions.description: The stated operating condition is above 1200 °C, whereas the proposed experiment is conducted at exactly 1200 °C, so the experiment does not strictly test the stated temperature domain.

The prediction requires at least a 50% mass-gain reduction, but the falsification rule only rejects the hypothesis when there is no significant difference. A significant reduction smaller than 50% would fail the quantitative prediction without satisfying the stated falsification rule.
